items.page: Subsets and Power Sets
items.caption: Three elements, three choices, eight subsets
items.text: Each level of the tree settles one element: follow the solid branch to keep it, the dashed branch to leave it out. Every path from the top makes exactly three choices and ends at a different subset — {a, b, c} when every element is kept, ∅ when none is. Two ways at each of three levels gives 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 paths, so {a, b, c} has 2³ = 8 subsets.

items.page: Cardinality
items.caption: The rule n ↦ 2n, on an infinite set and on a finite one
items.text: On the left every natural number n is sent to 2n, and every even number is hit exactly once — so ℕ pairs perfectly with the even numbers, a part of itself. On the right the same rule is tried on {0, 1, 2, 3} and its part {0, 2}: 2 and 3 are left with nowhere to go. A finite set can never pair with a proper part of itself; an infinite set always can.

items.page: Cardinality
items.caption: Listing the positive rationals
items.text: Each fraction p/q sits at column p, row q. The walk runs diagonal by diagonal, turning at the edges, so any fraction is reached after finitely many steps. A fraction not in lowest terms, such as 2/2, names a number already listed — it is dashed and gets no number, so every rational appears exactly once. The order numbers are the bijection with the natural numbers.

items.page: Cardinality
items.caption: Cantor's diagonal, five rows deep
items.text: Suppose the rows r₁, r₂, … list every number between 0 and 1. Take the n-th digit of the n-th row (boxed) and change it; those changed digits spell a new number x. x cannot be r₁ — they differ in the first digit; it cannot be r₂ — they differ in the second; and so on down every row. So no list is complete, and the reals are uncountable.

items.caption: A ∩ B under the Disjoint and A ⊆ B layouts
items.text: Under Disjoint the expression still selects the A ∩ B row, but that row has no area, so nothing shades. Under A ⊆ B it is the "A only" region that has no area. The region table is always 2^n rows; the drawing shows only the rows a layout admits.

items.secTitle: Three Sets and De Morgan's Law
items.caption: Three sets: A ∩ B ∩ C, then (A ∪ B)ᶜ
items.text: Eight regions. The triple intersection is one of them; the complement of A ∪ B is two - C alone and the area outside everything. Put A ᶜ ∩ B ᶜ in the Compare box and the tool reports them equivalent across all eight.
